misreadings.quote: she was the only one who didn't look away from the corpse
misreadings.evidence: Grete, who had not taken her eyes from the corpse, said: “Just look how thin he was.” ... Grete followed her parents into the bedroom but not without looking back at the body.
misreadings.explanation: The text says Grete also kept her eyes on the corpse and looked back at it, so the cleaner was not the only one who did not look away.

misreadings.quote: The sacking of the cleaner (n_47a37399) is the family’s first act of reclaimed decorum.
misreadings.evidence: “Tonight she gets sacked”, said Mr. Samsa, but he received no reply from either his wife or his daughter
misreadings.explanation: Mr. Samsa only says she will be sacked tonight, and no one answers him, so the dismissal has not happened yet; the reflection says 'By dismissing her' and the prose version says 'She is sacked almost immediately'.

misreadings.quote: They aren't mourning; they are 'synchronizing' with the spring.
misreadings.evidence: All of them had been crying a little; Grete now and then pressed her face against her father’s arm.
misreadings.explanation: The text shows the family crying a little just before this, so stating flatly that they are not mourning goes beyond what the text gives.

misreadings.quote: Mr. Samsa’s dismissive reference to Gregor’s life and death as 'all that old stuff'
misreadings.evidence: “Come here, then. Let’s forget about all that old stuff, shall we. Come and give me a bit of attention”.
misreadings.explanation: The text does not say what 'all that old stuff' refers to; the claim that it means Gregor's whole life, transformation and death is an interpretation stated as fact.

result.note: The main errors are that the cleaner is called the only one who did not look away from the corpse (Grete also kept looking) and that her sacking is treated as done when Mr. Samsa only says it will happen tonight.
